questions.question: Should I use RAG or fine-tuning for my LLM application?
questions.answer_summary: The practical framework: use RAG when failures come from missing or stale facts, and fine-tune when failures come from behavior inconsistency (wrong format, unstable tone, weak classification, poor policy adherence) — most sources agree RAG should be the default first choice for knowledge-heavy tasks.

questions.question: Does long context make RAG obsolete?
questions.answer_summary: No — while long-context windows are powerful, they are not an automatic replacement for retrieval pipelines; multiple analysts frame this explicitly as 'will RAG be killed by long-context LLMs?' and conclude RAG is 'maturing,' not dying, because it still offers attribution, cheaper updates, and model-swap flexibility.

questions.question: At what context length do long-context LLMs start to degrade on retrieval-heavy tasks?
questions.answer_summary: Databricks research found GPT-4-0125-preview's performance declines after 64k tokens and Llama-3.1-405B begins degrading at 32k tokens, while GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet stayed more consistent across longer contexts.

questions.question: Why does Claude sometimes refuse to answer at very long context lengths?
questions.answer_summary: Databricks found Claude-3-Sonnet increasingly refused to answer, citing copyright concerns, with a 49.5% failure rate at 64k tokens — attributed to insufficient long-context instruction-following training data.

questions.question: Do all models fail the same way when given too much context?
questions.answer_summary: No — failure patterns are model-specific: GPT-4 returns incorrect or irrelevant content, DBRX-Instruct defaults to summarizing instead of answering (50.4% failure at 32k), and Mixtral-8x7B generates repeated nonsensical or random characters.

questions.question: How does retrieval recall change as context size grows?
questions.answer_summary: Databricks found average recall across four datasets improved from 0.468 at 2k tokens to 0.95 at 192k tokens, showing that more retrieved documents genuinely helps up to a point before model-specific degradation kicks in.

questions.question: What percentage of production LLM problems actually require fine-tuning rather than RAG?
questions.answer_summary: A commonly cited figure is that roughly 70% of production problems don't need fine-tuning at all and can be solved with RAG, since RAG doesn't require significant compute and only needs domain-specific text data.

questions.question: Can teams combine RAG and fine-tuning instead of choosing one?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — mature systems increasingly use a hybrid: fine-tuning handles style/format/task-specific behavior while RAG supplies up-to-date, attributable knowledge, with the fine-tuned model acting as generator over RAG-provided context.

questions.question: What does a modern three-layer LLM architecture actually look like in 2026?
questions.answer_summary: One described architecture layers a small fine-tuned model for response format, a polished RAG pipeline with hybrid search and reranking for knowledge, and a 'Self-Route' layer that decides per-query whether retrieval is sufficient or full long context is needed.

questions.question: Is choosing between RAG and fine-tuning still the right question to ask in 2026?
questions.answer_summary: Practitioners argue the RAG-vs-fine-tuning framing is outdated; leading teams layer RAG (knowledge), fine-tuning (behavior), and long context (prototyping/edge cases) together with an evaluation framework to tell which piece is actually helping.

questions.question: How much data and compute does fine-tuning require compared to RAG?
questions.answer_summary: RAG doesn't require abundant computational resources and works with domain-specific text data alone, while fine-tuning requires adequate labeled data and meaningfully more compute to update model weights.

questions.question: When does fine-tuning clearly outperform RAG?
questions.answer_summary: Fine-tuning is favored for style, format consistency, narrow classification tasks, and cost efficiency at scale, once behavior (not missing knowledge) is the bottleneck.
